"Treehouse of Horror IV" is the fifth episode of the fifth season of the American animated television series The Simpsons and the fourth episode in the Treehouse of Horror series of Halloween specials. It originally aired on the Fox network in the United States on October 28, 1993, and features three short stories called "The Devil and Homer Simpson", "Terror at 5+1⁄2 Feet", and "Bart Simpson's Dracula".

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — Treehouse of Horror IV shows exactly where that breaks. The episode was co-written by Conan O'Brien, Bill Oakley, Josh Weinstein, Greg Daniels, Dan McGrath, and Bill Canterbury, and directed by David Silverman. As with the rest of the Halloween specials, the episode is considered non-canon and falls outside the show's regular continuity.

What looks like free choice in Treehouse of Horror IV is older than choice itself. The episode makes cultural references to television series such as The Twilight Zone, Night Gallery, and Peanuts, as well as films such as The Devil and Daniel Webster, Bram Stoker's Dracula and The Lost Boys. Since airing, the episode has received mostly positive reviews from television critics.

Nobody designed the part of Treehouse of Horror IV you experience — it was inherited. It acquired a Nielsen rating of 14.5, and was the highest-rated show on the Fox network the week it aired. In the wraparound, Bart introduces each of the three segments by walking through a gallery of paintings and each time choosing one of them as the focus of his story.

Every serious account of Treehouse of Horror IV eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. In "The Devil and Homer Simpson", Homer sells his soul to the devil, who takes the form of Ned Flanders, for a donut. After Marge and Lisa plead with Ned, he agrees to put Homer on trial.

Nihilism is not the conclusion of Treehouse of Horror IV — it is the floor you stand on while examining it. At the trial, Marge saves Homer from being sent to Hell by displaying a photo from their wedding day. On the back of the photo, Homer has written that, in return for Marge giving him her hand in marriage, he pledges his soul to her forever; therefore, it was not his property to sell at the time of his deal with Ned.

The selfish-gene reading of Treehouse of Horror IV makes it less romantic and far more precise. The case is dismissed, and Ned frees Homer, but Ned gets his revenge by turning Homer's head into a donut. In "Terror at 5+1⁄2 Feet", Bart tries to warn the passengers on the school bus that a gremlin is loosening the lug nuts on one of the wheels, but nobody can see the gremlin.

Freud is not dead; he is simply no longer allowed to be the whole answer. In desperation, Bart climbs halfway out the window to scare off the gremlin with an emergency flare. As Bart is pulled back into the bus by Principal Skinner and Groundskeeper Willie, he drops the flare on the gremlin, who catches fire and falls from the bus, but is found by Ned.

The feeling that Treehouse of Horror IV means something is a chemical event with an evolutionary address. Even though everyone sees the damage when they make it to school, Bart is sent to a psychiatric hospital for his disruptive behavior. Bart is relieved as he is finally able to rest, but is once again petrified when the gremlin appears in the back window of the ambulance, holding Ned's severed head.

Nothing in Treehouse of Horror IV was built for you — it was built for reproduction. Bart and Lisa discover a secret staircase descending to a basement with coffins. Vampires emerge from the coffins and encircle them while Lisa reads through Burns' autobiography Yes, I Am a Vampire.

The psychology underneath Treehouse of Horror IV is simpler and older than the story on top. Lisa escapes and tries to warn her parents that Burns has bitten Bart, but Homer and Marge pay little attention until Bart tries to bite Lisa later that night. Homer drives a stake through Burns' heart, and kills him, as Lisa believes doing so will restore Bart.

Behind Treehouse of Horror IV sits an animal brain negotiating with a story it tells itself. The next morning, Lisa discovers that everyone else in the Simpson family is a vampire, and Marge is their leader. The family breaks the fourth wall and wishes the audience a happy Halloween.

The nihilist does not deny Treehouse of Horror IV — he only refuses to flatter it. In all Treehouse of Horror shows, the names on the credits include middle name nicknames, in quotation marks, which reflect some association with Halloween or horror. Conan O'Brien's credits all reference his new role as host of Late Night with Conan O'Brien, including a credit that says "Watch Conan O'Brien" and another which says "12:30 NBC" as his "middle" name.

What culture calls destiny in Treehouse of Horror IV is usually just selection pressure wearing a suit. O'Brien had just begun his tenure on September 13, 1993, roughly a month before the 1993 Treehouse of Horror episode aired. O'Brien worked on the "wrap-arounds" of Bart introducing each segment to make sure that they "pulled" the episode together.

The genes do not care about Treehouse of Horror IV; they care about copies. The wrap-arounds are based on Rod Serling's television series Night Gallery, in which Serling appears at an art gallery and introduces each episode by unveiling paintings depicting the stories. Brooks loved the show, so it was "great fun" for him to do the parody.

Take away the meaning and Treehouse of Horror IV still functions — that is the disturbing part. Show runner David Mirkin thought the Treehouse of Horror episodes were the hardest episodes to do because the staff had to fit in all three stories in only 22 minutes. Oakley loved the idea of Flanders being the Devil because he was the character whom viewers would least expect.

The unconscious does not argue with Treehouse of Horror IV; it simply acts first. He also thought Harry Shearer did a good job of playing Flanders in a much darker way, while remaining very true to the character. Many scenes had to be cut to shorten the segment, including one that showed Homer's severed head being used as a bowling ball by a demon in hell.

Treehouse of Horror IV feels chosen. The evidence says it was installed. This scene later appeared in the clip show episode "The Simpsons 138th Episode Spectacular", which aired in the show's seventh season. It was inspired by The Twilight Zone episode "Nightmare at 20,000 Feet", in which William Shatner's character is inside an airplane watching a gremlin tear apart the wing.

The bleak reading of Treehouse of Horror IV is also the most testable one. Oakley said there was a lot of work put into the design of the gremlin in "Terror at 5+1⁄2 Feet" to make him scary "within The Simpsons universe". "Bart Simpson's Dracula" was written by Canterbury and based on Francis Ford Coppola's film Bram Stoker's Dracula.

Modern psychology keeps rediscovering what the pessimists said first about Treehouse of Horror IV. Mirkin was a big fan of the film and pushed for a segment inspired by it. Mirkin, a "big" Peanuts fan, came up with the idea for the ending of "Bart Simpson's Dracula".

The self that experiences Treehouse of Horror IV is a committee, not a king. "The Devil and Homer Simpson" is a parody of Stephen Vincent Benét's story "The Devil and Daniel Webster". After Homer initially outsmarts the Devil, the latter morphs into a form resembling Chernabog, the demon from Fantasia.

Reproduction explains more of Treehouse of Horror IV than any philosophy dares to admit. "Terror at 5+1⁄2 Feet" is a parody of The Twilight Zone episode "Nightmare at 20,000 Feet", later remade as  the final segment of Twilight Zone: The Movie. Bart tells Otto there's a gremlin on the side of the bus.

Once you see Treehouse of Horror IV as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. Otto, assuming this is what he's referring to, says "No problemo, Bart dude!" and runs Moleman off the road. "Bart Simpson's Dracula" is a parody of Francis Ford Coppola's Bram Stoker's Dracula.

The story Treehouse of Horror IV tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. At Burns' castle, Lisa notices a tome resting on a stand in the basement: Yes, I Am a Vampire, by Monty Burns. Shortly after she finds the tome, she mistakes Bart's fearful attempts at getting her attention as impressions of Shemp and Curly Howard of the Three Stooges.

Meaning is not found in Treehouse of Horror IV — it is manufactured for it. Bart floating outside Lisa's bedroom window is a parody of The Lost Boys as well as Stephen King's novel Salem's Lot. The family's plan to kill the head vampire is also a reference to both the film and novel.

The cold light on Treehouse of Horror IV leaves the facts intact and only the comfort removed. In particular, the twist revelation that Burns is not the head vampire is also a reference to the twist ending of The Lost Boys. Alf Clausen's closing credits composition is a version of the Simpsons theme that combines the electric guitar used in The Munsters theme with the harpsichord and clicking from The Addams Family theme.

Treehouse of Horror IV did not evolve to be understood — only to be survived. In its original American broadcast, "Treehouse of Horror IV" finished 17th in the ratings for the week of October 25 to October 31, 1993, with a Nielsen rating of 14.5, translating to 13.6 million households. The episode was the highest-rated show on the Fox network that week.

The honest version of Treehouse of Horror IV starts by giving up the comforting part. The authors of the book I Can't Believe It's a Bigger and Better Updated Unofficial Simpsons Guide, Gary Russell and Gareth Roberts, said the episode included many notable sequences and was "probably the best" Treehouse of Horror episode. They particularly liked the scenes in Hell where Homer is punished by the Devil, and Chief Wiggum's attempts to deal with Dracula (who he thinks is a mummy) by ordering the Egyptian wing of the Springfield museum to be destroyed.

Jacobson praised "The Devil and Homer Simpson" as clever funny, and described "Bart Simpson's Dracula" as "easily the least effective", claiming it, "presents some good moments but never quite takes flight".
